titleStmt.title: Memorandum by the United States Delegation at the Council of Foreign Ministers

head.hi: Memorandum by the United States Delegation at the Council of Foreign Ministers

div.p:
In discussing the German problem, it seems to the United States Delegation that it must be considered in two parts. The first of these
is clarification of policies and principles agreed between the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Republic [Union] at Potsdam which are short range in character. The second part is the plan for the long-range implementation of Potsdam. The latter must look forward to the eventual provision of peace terms to the German nation. The views of the United States Delegation relative to the preparation of this plan are included in a paper which is now passed for circulation.

It would appear, however, that some immediate problems remain to permit the accomplishment of the short-range objectives envisaged in the Potsdam Protocol. While the level of industry to be left in Germany has been agreed in the Control Council, this agreement is based on the treatment of Germany as an economic unit. I am advised that many of the plants to be removed under this plan have already been declared, and that within a short period the remaining plants will be declared as available for reparations. Thus it is possible at an early date to press vigorously the dismantling and delivering of the agreed capital equipment.

However, since this plan is conditioned upon the treatment of Germany as an economic unit, requisite procedure for this purpose must be established before dismantling is placed into operation. Otherwise, the US Zone and, I am sure, other zones would be left in a position which would create a definite financial liability which we at least are not prepared to accept.
It is understood that the French have already raised the question of the Saar and its permanent control by France as a reservation in the declaring of plants available for reparations.

Hence it would appear that the following questions must be resolved before the reparations program can be advanced. These questions are: (1)
Will consideration be given to the internationalization of the Ruhr and Rhineland, and if some form of internationalization is agreed, will the resources of the Ruhr and Rhineland remain as a part of the German economic structure? (2)
Will the resources left in Germany be made available for Germany as a whole, and will those resources surplus to minimum German requirements be made available for export with the proceeds being applied in the first instance to meet agreed essential imports for Germany as a whole? (3)
Can agreed procedures for sufficient German administrative machinery to permit its operation as an economic unit be established during the next ninety days? (4)
Will the existing zonal boundaries be continued only for purposes of delineating occupation areas and not as artificial barriers to a reasonably free movement of goods in Germany?
(5)
Can a tentative agreement be reached for inclusion in the peace treaty as to the final limits of the western boundary of German?

These questions must be answered if the de-industrialization program of Germany is to be carried out now. It has become apparent that they must be settled at this Council as the basic questions are beyond the competence of the Allied Control Council.

It is my recommendation that these questions be referred to our Deputies so that their recommendations may be placed before the Council of Foreign Ministers at its June 15 session. If this is agreed, I do not believe that we would need to delay further in the allocation of plants and in starting to dismantle the plants now declared for reparations, as the work to this end undertaken prior to our next meeting would not be irreparable if agreement could not be reached.
I urge earnestly, therefore, that these questions be considered by our Deputies in broad principle so that the Allied Control Council may be given the necessary guidance to continue its work.

While these questions are being considered I think it is also time to plan now for the peace terms to be granted at some later date to the German people. The procedure for the development of such a plan recommended by the United States Delegation is outlined in the paper which you have before you.
